title: Union Minister Bandi Sanjay's Son Arrested in POCSO Case as Father Vows 'No One Above the Law'
excerpt: The arrest of a BJP Union minister's son on child sexual abuse charges tests the party's zero-tolerance rhetoric and raises questions about accountability in India's political dynasties
body:
## A Political Family's Reckoning

When Union Minister of State for Home Affairs Bandi Sanjay Kumar publicly declared he was "handing over" his own son to the police, it marked one of the most dramatic moments in recent Indian political life. The arrest of his son by Telangana police under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act has sent shockwaves through the BJP's ranks, testing the party's oft-proclaimed commitment to law and order—and raising uncomfortable questions about accountability in India's political dynasties.

### The Arrest and the Minister's Response

Telangana police arrested Bandi Sanjay's son on charges filed under the stringent POCSO Act, which governs cases of sexual offences against minors. The specifics of the allegations remain under investigation, but the severity of the charges—POCSO cases carry a minimum sentence of five years—underscores the gravity of the situation.

In a carefully worded statement, the senior Sanjay Kumar struck a tone of stoic compliance. "All are equal before the law," he told reporters, adding that he had personally ensured his son's cooperation with authorities. The minister's attempt to frame the arrest as an act of principled compliance has been met with both praise from some quarters and skepticism from opposition parties who question whether the same standard would apply absent media scrutiny.

### A Pattern in Indian Politics

The case has reignited a familiar debate about political families and legal accountability in India. From the Lalu Prasad family's corruption trials to the periodic entanglements of the Karunanidhi and Badal clans, the intersection of political power and criminal justice remains one of Indian democracy's most fraught fault lines.

What distinguishes this case is the severity of the charge. POCSO cases occupy a particularly sensitive space in Indian jurisprudence—courts have consistently held that the Act's protections for minors must override all other considerations, including the status of the accused's family. Legal experts note that any perception of special treatment could trigger judicial intervention.

### The BJP's Political Calculus

For the ruling party, the timing is particularly inopportune. The BJP has built significant political capital on its tough-on-crime narrative, and Bandi Sanjay himself rose to prominence as the party's combative Telangana president who led aggressive campaigns against the then-ruling TRS government. Having a Union minister's son face POCSO charges creates a dissonance that opposition parties are already exploiting.

The Congress party and the Bharat Rashtra Samithi (BRS) have both demanded that Sanjay Kumar step down from his ministerial position during the investigation—a demand the BJP has so far rejected, arguing that the charges are against his son, not the minister himself.

### What NRIs Should Watch

For the Indian diaspora, this case crystallises a recurring concern about governance and institutional integrity back home. NRIs who follow Indian politics—particularly those who fund political campaigns or engage in advocacy—are acutely aware that the credibility of India's legal institutions depends on cases like these being handled without fear or favour.

The POCSO Act, enacted in 2012, was itself partly a response to international pressure and diaspora advocacy following high-profile child abuse cases. Its implementation remains uneven across states, with conviction rates varying dramatically. How Telangana's judiciary handles a case involving a powerful political family will be closely watched as a barometer of institutional independence.

### What Comes Next

The investigation is ongoing, and Bandi Sanjay's son will face formal judicial proceedings in the coming weeks. The minister has signalled he will not seek to interfere, though political observers note that the real test will come if the case progresses toward trial. Historically, POCSO cases involving politically connected families have faced delays and procedural complications—a pattern that advocacy groups will be watching carefully.

For now, the episode serves as a stark reminder that India's political class, however powerful, operates within a legal framework that can still—at least occasionally—assert its authority without regard to status or station.
